blocks.content: Direct access to the matrix elements related to decays is missing in the Euclidean formulations of lattice QCD.
The price to be paid is that the relevant symmetry group in the lattice calculation is signiﬁcantly reduced.

Other studies of ππ I = 2 scattering in lattice QCD ([23–25]) have largely limited themselves to the threshold behavior of the scat- tering amplitude in S-wave, as expressed by the scatter- ing length.

blocks.content:
QCD is the accepted underlying theory of the strong
interactions, and the properties of the spectrum and in-
teractions of hadrons should be calculable from it using
a suitable regularization scheme for the quark and gluon

the theory on a ﬁnite lattice of space-time points so as to
admit a numerical method of solution. While signiﬁcant
progress has been made recently in determining the single
particle spectrum of hadrons, describing the resonances
seen in scattering experiments in terms of eigenstates of

blocks.title: VIII Phase-shifts from finite-volume spectra
blocks.content:
SPECTRA
The formalism to relate the amplitude for two-particle
elastic scattering in partial waves labelled by angular mo-
mentum ℓ, to the spectrum of states in a ﬁnite cubic spa-
tial volume, is laid down in [2], with extensions to the
case of a moving frame presented in [16–18].
Because
we are considering ππ scattering in isospin-2 where only
even ℓoccur, there is a one-to-one correspondence be-
tween the irreps of the symmetry group relevant for the
L¨uscher formalism in a moving frame and the little group
irreps13 and so we will refer to the little group irreps.
The formalism can be compa

In order to demonstrate the formalism, we will brieﬂy break away from analysis of lattice QCD obtained ﬁnite- volume spectra to consider a simple toy-model of ππ scat- tering in which the scattering amplitudes are known to us.

The problem to be solved in lattice QCD is actually the inverse of that just described - we start with the ﬁnite-volume spectrum determined through analysis of correlation functions and want to ﬁnd the phase-shifts as a function of scattering momentum.
We do not present this trivial result here, but we will return to this “global ﬁtting” method in the next section when we consider the ﬁnite-volume spectrum obtained from lattice QCD computations.
